name: Text to SQL
title: Text to SQL
answer: Text to SQL is the task of translating a natural language question into a SQL query that runs against a real schema and returns the answer, and it is how business users query data without an analyst in between. The question arrives in ordinary language, the system resolves it against tables, columns, keys and joins it has been shown, and the output is a statement the database engine will accept. Success is judged by whether the query runs and whether the rows it returns answer the question that was asked, which are two different tests. A query can execute cleanly and still be wrong, and a query can be right in intent but fail on a type mismatch or an ambiguous column name.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The system needs the schema itself, meaning table and column names, data types, primary and foreign keys, and often a few sample rows or column descriptions so the model can tell a status code from a customer name. Most deployments keep a semantic layer or a curated set of table and column descriptions, because raw schemas are terse and full of abbreviations that mean nothing outside the team that built them. Retrieval is usually part of the stack, selecting the handful of tables relevant to the question before any generation happens, since a large warehouse will not fit in a prompt. The generated SQL then runs against a read replica or a sandboxed copy rather than production, with a row limit and a timeout attached.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The common pattern is retrieval over schema and past queries, then generation by a language model, then execution, then a check on the result. Teams improve accuracy with a library of verified question and query pairs used as examples, and with feedback from users who mark an answer as right or wrong. Evaluation is done on held out questions with known correct results, and the useful metrics are execution accuracy, meaning the query ran and returned the expected rows, and exact match, meaning the query text matched a reference. Exact match is the weaker signal because two different queries can return the same correct answer. Errors cluster around joins, grouping, date handling and the model inventing a column that does not exist.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The generated query runs with the permissions of whoever or whatever executes it, so a text to SQL layer can widen access if it is wired to a privileged account. The usual control is to run under the asking user's own credentials, or to restrict the layer to views and columns that user is already entitled to see. Every generated query should be logged with the question, the SQL, the user and the row count, both for debugging and for audit. Sensitive columns such as identifiers, health details or payment data need explicit exclusion rather than a hope that the model will not select them. Where the output feeds a report or a decision, a human review step is common, and the provenance of the answer, meaning which tables and filters produced it, should be visible to the person reading it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Accuracy on real, messy schemas is the main open problem, and progress is coming from better schema retrieval, from models fine tuned on SQL, and from agent style loops that run a query, read the error and try again. Benchmarks have moved from small single table sets to large multi table warehouses with ambiguous column names and dialect differences, which is closer to what practitioners actually face. The direction of travel is toward the layer sitting inside the warehouse and the BI tool rather than beside them, so the question, the query and the chart stay in one place. The unresolved questions are how much autonomy to grant, how to keep the semantic layer current as schemas change, and how to show a user why an answer is trustworthy without asking them to read SQL.
